notes.meaning: The Jewish council stood up and brought Jesus before Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Under Roman law, the Jewish court was not allowed to carry out an execution. They needed the Roman ruler to approve the death sentence and order Jesus to be put to death.

The religious leaders knew Pilate would not care about Jewish religious arguments. So they brought three political accusations against Jesus to make Him sound like a dangerous rebel against Rome. They falsely claimed that He led people into rebellion, told them not to pay taxes, and claimed to be an earthly king.

Pilate asked Jesus directly if He was the King of the Jews, because a rival king was a threat to Rome. Jesus answered that it was as Pilate said, accepting the title while pointing to a spiritual kingdom rather than an earthly rebellion. His calm answer made it clear that He was not leading a violent revolt.

Pilate spoke openly to the chief priests and the crowd, declaring that Jesus had committed no crime. He saw that Jesus had no army and posed no political danger to Caesar. Under Roman law, there was no legal ground to punish Him.

The accusers grew louder and pressed harder when they saw their case failing. They claimed Jesus was stirring up trouble all over the country, from Galilee all the way to Jerusalem. They mentioned Galilee on purpose, knowing that Pilate feared the rebellions that often started in that region.

When Pilate heard the word Galilee, he asked whether Jesus came from that region. He was looking for any legal way to escape a hard decision. If Jesus belonged to another ruler, Pilate could avoid angering the crowd or executing an innocent man.

Once Pilate learned that Jesus came from Galilee, he sent Him to Herod Antipas, the ruler over that area. Herod was in Jerusalem at that time to take part in the Passover feast. Pilate saw this as a chance to pass the case to Herod while showing him political respect.

Herod was very glad to see Jesus because he had heard about Him for a long time. He had no desire to repent or learn the truth. Instead, he treated Jesus like an entertainer and hoped to watch Him perform a miracle for amusement.

Herod asked Jesus many questions, but Jesus did not give Him a single word in reply. Jesus had always answered honest seekers and healed the needy, but He refused to speak just to please a cruel king's curiosity. His quiet dignity fulfilled the ancient prophecy that the Lord's servant would be silent like a lamb before its shearers.

The chief priests and teachers of the law stood in Herod's court, shouting violent accusations against Jesus. They had followed Jesus there because they were afraid Herod might set Him free. Their loud charges showed how desperate and determined they were to see Him condemned.

Because Jesus would not perform for him, Herod and his soldiers treated Him as foolish and worthless. They put an elegant, bright robe on Him to make fun of His claim to be a king. Then Herod sent Him right back to Pilate without finding Him guilty of any capital crime.

Pilate and Herod became friends on that very day, ending a long quarrel. Pilate's polite act of sending Jesus to Herod healed the bad feelings between them. Worldly rulers who agree on little else often unite in their opposition to Christ and His kingdom.

After Jesus was returned, Pilate called together the chief priests, the Jewish rulers, and the ordinary people. He wanted everyone present so he could announce his official verdict before the whole community. He also hoped that some among the crowd might speak up in favor of Jesus.

Pilate reminded the leaders that they had accused Jesus of leading the people in revolt. He stated that he had questioned Jesus thoroughly right in front of them. After a complete legal examination, he found no evidence to support any of their political charges.

Pilate pointed out that Herod had reached the very same conclusion. Herod was familiar with Jewish customs and had also questioned Jesus, but he sent Him back without finding any crime. Both rulers had examined Jesus, and both confirmed that He had done nothing deserving death.

Pilate suggested a compromise by offering to whip Jesus and then set Him free. Roman scourging was a cruel and bloody beating, and it was wrong to punish a prisoner who was entirely innocent. Pilate offered this lesser punishment hoping to satisfy the angry mob while saving Jesus from death.
Pilate referred to the established custom of releasing one Jewish prisoner during the annual Passover feast. He hoped the crowd would choose Jesus, giving him a clean way to let an innocent man go.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The earliest Greek manuscripts do not contain this verse, suggesting it was originally a reader's note drawn from the accounts in Matthew and Mark to explain the custom.

notes.meaning: The crowd shouted back together with one voice, demanding that Jesus be taken away to die. They rejected Pilate's offer of mercy and insisted that he execute Jesus. Instead of Jesus, they asked the governor to release a prisoner named Barabbas.

Barabbas was a dangerous criminal who had been thrown into prison for taking part in an armed revolt and for murder. The crowd demanded freedom for a violent killer while seeking the death of the peaceful Son of God.

Pilate spoke to the people again because he still wanted to set Jesus free. He tried to reason with them and turn them away from their murderous demand. Yet he lacked the courage to uphold justice on his own authority.

The crowd drowned out Pilate's words by yelling over and over that Jesus should be crucified. Crucifixion was a horrific and shameful Roman method of execution meant for slaves and rebels. The people were so filled with hatred that they would accept nothing less than Jesus' death on a cross.

For the third time, Pilate asked the crowd what wrong Jesus had actually done. He stated again that he found no crime in Jesus that deserved execution. He repeated his offer to whip Jesus and let Him go, desperately looking for an escape from their demands.

The people refused to listen and grew more urgent, shouting at the top of their lungs for crucifixion. Their loud screams fell upon Pilate like a violent storm. In the end, the noise and anger of the crowd overpowered the governor's will.

Pilate gave up the struggle and officially granted the crowd's demand. He chose to protect his own political career and avoid a riot rather than defend an innocent man. He gave the legal order for Jesus to be put to death.

Pilate set free the man who had been locked up for rebellion and murder, exactly as the crowd requested. Then he surrendered Jesus to be beaten, mocked, and killed according to their wishes. In this trade, a guilty rebel went free while the sinless Savior took his place, picturing how Christ dies in the place of sinners.

Roman soldiers led Jesus away toward the site of execution. Jesus was weak from severe beatings, so the soldiers forced a man named Simon from Cyrene in North Africa to carry the heavy crossbeam behind Him.
A large crowd followed Jesus along the road, including many women from Jerusalem. These women were filled with sorrow at His terrible suffering, weeping aloud and beating their chests in deep grief.

Jesus turned toward the weeping women and told them not to weep for Him, but for themselves and their children. Even on the way to the cross, His thoughts were on the future suffering of others. He knew that awful judgment and destruction would soon fall on Jerusalem because the nation had rejected God's mercy.
